Bringing back so that the assets that you find in Africa can now be invested in. So that, for me, gives me confidence that for the first time, African institutions are not waiting for a prescription. The second is that the private sector there has decided that actually we're going to seed our wealth in Africa, not outside of the continent. And that's being done by a wealthy billionaire there who is getting traction because suddenly everybody's looking to, so if he's made so much money, he's now vesting that opportunity on the continent.
The Nigerian billionaire.

Of course, I come from Nigeria, you know. Nigerian billionaire. But I think what is capturing the imagination there is the sale of the IPO that he did the other day to the ordinary person who now sees that they also have ownership of what is now going to be a huge amount of development for them. It's going to be jobs. It is going to be a chance that people will hope to get past the conflict because there's an alternative. There are lots of TikTok jokes and cartoons about him that show him asking a poor person, why are you touching my vehicle? You know, the truck that carries the petroleum. And the poor person's just saying to him, it's our truck. So people feel an ownership in that business. If we could translate that, now this is where it gets complicated. Political will for me is about leadership. And there are very few leaders who've got the opportunity to do things are doing anything about it, and the ones that don't have the opportunity is where all the leadership is. But here, I think that we need to see every citizen say that to their leaders, that, you know, we have a shareholding in this entity called Nigeria. And in response to that, you've got to deliver. And this has to happen in sufficient number of countries, particularly in those that have and are just closing the doors to try to open them up. The financing needs to open up. We have frameworks, we have goals, we have toolboxes. There's nothing that we don't have. Jeffrey Sachs has been at this for the best part of, I don't know, 40, 50 years, but of recent, at least the 10 years on the SDGs. The SDGs spoke to us having inclusive economies, and it's about the economy. If you can't grow an economy, you will not get the revenue to pay for a health system. You can't keep borrowing for that from ODA that's gone down by 28%. You need to invest in infrastructure, you need to invest in power, you need to invest in what will kick that economy so that they can get the revenues to do what they should basically do as rights and then everyone will get started. I know we'll talk about AI later, but I just want to talk about the opportunity of that. But right now, I think Africa is showing the way on the finance and it's taken that leaf from severe. It's taken that leaf from Bridgetown because we tackle the MDBs. We tackled the IMF.

So essentially, it's about the economy, stupid, right? Always. It's always about the economy. Prime Minister Sanchez, looking back at severe, what's the one lesson that should change how we approach financing next, especially with military spending rising and geopolitical tensions deepening? What needs to change about how we finance the SDGs.

Well, to me, the political priorities, I mean, I think that precisely in the Western societies, in Western countries and governments, now, I come from a country, Spain, that belongs to the European Union. Of course, we have the threat of Russia and the war in Ukraine. But of course, you know, we are against not only that illegal war, but the war in Iran. And of course, what is going on in Gaza in Palestine. So I think that first of all, we need to change our political priorities in Western societies. And for that, we need governments more engaged on global issues, but also societies that understand that geopolitics also affects directly to their daily lives. And then I feel, and this is my My biggest concern is that more and more, since we have this rearming rhetoric, we are forgetting to be engaged on global matters that affect us. also when it comes to, for instance, migration, we need also to cooperate with countries of origin and transit, but not only regarding migration, but the economic development of these countries. So I can give a lot of examples, but I would say that the biggest lesson that to me was Seville. It was a light to change political priorities, especially when it comes to Western societies and Western governments.

I saw the wheels turning, but let me ask you this first. You've been one of the leading voices, Prime Minister Motley, on calling for reform of the global financial system. Looking ahead, where should leaders focus their energy now, changing the rules or changing the incentives that determine where capital flows?

The reality is that I don't think we're going to see what we want happen in one fell swoop. We're going to see incremental changes we've been doing. I'd like it to be far greater. But against that backdrop, I think leaders need to be taking action where they can. And that's why I said that the debt swaps, you referred to them just now, Barbados has successfully managed two debt swaps. It's now doing its third debt swap. In fact, we're doing the first debt for social swap that will conclude on the 31st of December, where we've brought four multilateral development banks together to work with us to repurchase 600 million US of our debt. And the savings from that is 150 million US, which would be applied across a three-year to the health institutions of the country. We're also using and insisting that the debt clauses be used. The debt pause clause alliance that Pedro spoke about is real. Look, everybody told us, oh, you're going to get that from concessional loans, etcetera, but the market will never give it to you. We went to the market last year in June and we raised 500 million US dollars and we got debt pause and pandemic clauses in those bonds raised on the international market having done road from Boston to New York to London to Paris. So we have to stop believing that these things are impossible. And if leaders can take action where they can, then that inspires others to believe that we can actually have this integrated across the place. The V2V compact is so important because you cannot pay But for serious institutions with 10 and 12 year money. And I keep making the point that home ownership became revolutionized when people had access to mortgages because they were borrowing at terms and conditions that were reflective of the life of the asset. It's common sense. So I can't get away from the absence of the political will. But equally, I know that once you can claim territory where you can, the longest mile begins with what? The first step. And we just have to show what is possible. And equally, why the V2V comeback is so important. It's the global south that effectively started it to work with the global south. And it shows that what is possible. How in all conscience can you charge people more interest rates because they are greater risk? That's exactly when you should be helping them. And it runs contrary to every single religion that we have.

I think that's an applause line. If no one was paying attention, I would just-- DSG, for too many countries, progress still feels out of reach. What will it take to turn today's financing commitments into results that people can actually see and feel? I mean, that is essentially the point of the SDGs, is it not?

It is, but it comes back to the means of implementation. I mean, we sort of got the needle stuck, right, so we know exactly what we need to do. And I think perhaps the narrative needs to change as to why we shouldn't do it. There's always an excuse as to why there's too much risk and who's going to take the risk and how are we going to raise the capital.
And those credit ratings agencies?

And credit rating agencies that also need a few lessons. And I think that's begun. We had put a big spotlight on credit rating agencies again through the SIVs. And I think now they are coming to stable, not as much as they should, the top three, but Africa says, "I'm not waiting think we're going to launch a credit rating agency. Is that going to solve the problem? Probably not. There's over 100 of them. But it will start to task those who have held everyone to ransom about how we're going to do this. And I think that if you look at the domestic resources that our countries use, that's the vast amount of resources being used for development right now. It's just not enough. And how we scale that has been the big question. How we actually put the footprint of the international community in countries to help them start to look at the policy and the regulatory environments and all those issues that we quite frankly don't tackle and target the G20 or target the G7. We do it for climate, this is where the emissions are, so these are the countries that we're negotiating with, so why do we not do that on the finance front? Often those rooms developing countries are locked out of might be there in the G 20, but in the G 20, these are a couple of pretty big countries, right, that are from the south. The G seven needs to be, you know, they need to take this on. And, you know, often people are not in those rooms. And yet they have so much impact within the financial system, within the multilateral development banks. So I don't think that we can get the I don't think we can get those resources without some changes really being made where it requires not just the political leadership, but some leaders as we had a decade or so ago in the financial crisis to take some decisions. We've had it with the SDRs, there are one or two countries that did that, but somehow that last mile of additional did not happen. So who are going to be the advocates of a new narrative that actually that four, five billion people that we talk about matter? And if you look at the rhetoric or the speeches we had in the hall today, it's very worrying. It's worrying that in the United Nations today that we will have speech that will come out with talking about the annihilation of people in an institution that was set up off the back of a war to have no more wars and to have peace. So, what are we thinking about? And we're talking about the SDGs, 2030 is around the corner. So when you tell me the financing, the financing is in the hands of too few and it needs to get out.

I will just say I come from a country that has recently been excluded from the room and referring to the G20, but that's a conversation for another time. DSG, let me just linger with you, but there's growing momentum around measuring progress beyond GDP. If we made that shift, what should change and how about how we define and finance a successful SDG agenda?

Well, the SDG agenda, the core of it has got our transitions to a greener, bluer, turquoise environment. I mean, sustainability, right? And sustainability today is rewarded by GDP, where fossil fuel is, that's, you get rewarded for it. So what we're trying to say is to bring in those issues that are for sustainability, bring in wellbeing, bringing all the issues that at the end of the day is about human dignity. And the price on that today is too high because we are measuring in a manner in which gives incentives for what we shouldn't be doing. And what we need is disincentives, and the GDP plus is lots of disincentives for what's not so good.

I will say we've got about four minutes and 30 seconds left. Let's see how much we can get through. Prime Minister Markley, many people hear discussions about debt restructuring, special drawing rights, multilateral development bank reform, and they struggle to connect them to daily life. How do these reforms ultimately translate into tangible benefits for people, whether through jobs, resilience, economic opportunity, or stronger public services?

Very clearly. If I have to build a hospital. with 15-year money, it means that my debt repayments for that hospital are much more than they should be. It means that I then have to choose what I can do and what I can't do. And that is the explanation that we have to give our people so that they understand that what we're fighting for is really about creating more opportunities for them in terms of education, healthcare, jobs, et cetera. We have to be able to get that space because we can always bring back down debt overnight, but we can't reverse if generation that has been lost overnight, they're gone. So that we don't have that luxury. And I think that we have to be able to be very, very clear that what we're doing is not an academic discussion. And that's why taking the tangible steps that we're doing with the V2V, trying to get longer, cheaper money for education, health, and water is so important. Now, that's not going to cover all of the SDGs, but it's going to carry us a large and long way being able to make progress. And that is real for my citizens and the rest of the citizens of the world.
I would argue, Prime Minister, that you're a very good communicator. So I wonder just how, as you've just done, connecting those dots to people.
300 million instead of 300,000.
But for the people--.

Because that's when I can make a difference. And Amina made the point. The problem is, is that where leadership is coming from the global south, they don't have the capacity or the power. And there's a power imbalance. And if you want me to be very precise and very brutal, the same men's rear that spawned slavery is the same men's rear that is maintaining the imbalance in the global environment, maintaining the imbalance in the power structure in this organization, maintaining the imbalance in the power structure in the national financial institution. How can you tell me there's a right to have a Security Council that don't have a representative from Africa as of right, or don't have a representative from the small island developing states that constitute one quarter of the world's states? Something is fundamentally wrong and we all know it, but what are we doing about it?
Speaking to you and amplifying that around the world.

Speaking to the media, advocacy. But at the end of the day, go to the rules and see where the rules are changed. And the rules are only changed when those who have access to power do it, or you get a moment like the let them eat bread moment, let them eat cakes moment, when people stand up and recognize that we're no longer listening to a handful of people who have excluded us from the conversation and that we have nothing to lose. When it gets to that point, we're risking danger. And that's why this whole conversation at the end of the day, whether it is global inequality, whether it is AI that will consolidate potentially the inequity, even while promising to create opportunities for other people. These are real things that cannot be decided by the power brokers who get the interest and make the money and the profits to the exclusion of everybody else in the world. This is a global conversation and people cannot be excluded from it.

So from the French Revolution to this question, Prime Minister, and I'm going to allow you to end with a flourish. We've got 55 seconds left. As we get closer to 2030, should our focus be solely, and it's an interesting question, should it be solely on accelerating delivery towards that deadline on today's agenda, or is it time to start preparing for what comes next?

Both. No, I think that we have to deliver. Four years in politics is a universe, so we need to focus. And of course, the causes of fighting against inequality, gender equality, green transition, climate change, these are causes that will go beyond 2030. But to me, I will echo what Mia said. I think it's very important to know that this is a political battle, not an ideological one, but a political one. Because many times we find people and political representatives that say, oh, this Agenda 2030 is for the global elite. And precisely is the contrary. this is the agenda for ordinary people. And I think that, you know, with concrete examples and with concrete policies, we have to fight against this narrative. And by the way, this Agenda 2030 is not only for, you know, countries less developed, but also in Western societies, we need the Agenda 2030 domestically. And this is something that we need to also expand this message to create this partnership with the academia, with business people, with trade unions, with civil society in order to expand the message within Western societies that the Agenda 2030 is for the good of the ordinary people, also from those societies.

I really want to see you, because we talked about political will and the way to go but he has lived it and he's shown it. Sevilla only happened because he was supportive of Sevilla happening. The manner in which he is treating the migrants in Spain is only because he has the political will to treat them differently. And he is therefore showing by the way in which he's walking that it is possible to do the right thing while at the same time providing for your citizens and making sure that the declining and aging populations of Europe do not undermine the growth potential of Europe.
I've been given an extra two minutes to talk about AI, so maybe we'll go down. down the panel. Prime Minister, you want to start? There's no question. I mean, where does AI lead you?
I will answer with a question. Okay.
You want to go first? Okay.

In 20th century, we wouldn't allow the private company to own a nuclear arsenal. Are we going to do that in the 21st century with the tool AI, this intelligence? and its implications, not only economically, but social and security implications for all humanity. That is the big question that we need to answer.
So if it was a car, we need a seatbelt.

No, we need regulation. Joseph Stiglitz made, I think, a very good point in his last article in the Financial Times. He said, look, we need an agenda for AI, which means competition, regulation, and redistribution. And I agree with that.

And I would only add to that, that at the time when we have the global town hall, for us to leave New York, without agreeing in the same way that we have done. We're not going to get every country on earth, but we need to be able to have the majority of countries saying, we agree that there must be regulation. We put a task force to get the framework for it, and that we are urging every country by the end of this year to put their domestic regulations in place without prejudice to what can be agreed to internationally.
Final word, DC.

So the UN is doing something about it. I think we faced a huge pushback from people we never expected it from to bring the governance in here, to bring the science in here, and to bring the dialogue. And more recently, what does it mean to be human in the age of AI? Better still, as we are meeting here now, the Security Council is meeting on AI. And I think that that has happened over the last week when there have been all these signals that this is not something that you would just give to a few companies. We had a nuclear treaty, we need an AI treaty. And that's what's being discussed right now downstairs. We were asking, inviting all those tech companies to come to the UN for the GA a couple of weeks ago. They were not coming. But they're here now, and they're in the Security Council. And I think that that's a huge step forward. And it just underscores how important multilateralism is, that when we cannot find and we need to pull together as a world to find a response to these huge challenges, this is where it happens. So I'm hopeful. And I hope that downstairs, they will come out with something that we go home with, that we can begin to work on. That conversation wasn't here a week ago. It is today. Good old UN.
Good old UN. I have to ask. You don't have a mic. We don't have a mic for you.
He doesn't need one.
I'm not mic'd, but I want to say these.
Are-- Professor Jeffrey Sachs, everybody.

-Three finest leaders that we have. And every one of them has taken incredible risks. And incredible-- These are the three finest leaders we have. Every one of them has taken incredible risks. every day and including this year and this month, and we depend on them for what they're doing. The majority is there in this world, in fact, the vast majority. But you saw the opponent this morning. So I would use a different word. The two words is not political will, but United States. This is a serious problem. But the vast majority of the world wants peace. wants the UN to function, wants the development agenda to be fulfilled, wants the climate change to be addressed, wants safety for the people of the world. We have a political obstacle. We don't lack the political will, and we have great political leaders, and the three best are here. So thank you.

All that's left for me to say is this. Prime Minister Markley, Prime Minister Sanchez, Deputy Secretary General, Mina Mohammed, thank you for a rich discussion. We've heard about the importance of turning momentum into implementation, ensuring that financing reaches where it is needed most, and keeping people at the center of efforts to reform the global financial system. Thank you for joining us, and thank you for the rich discussion. See you back here tomorrow, same time. Thank you, thank you.
